title: CBSE Class 12 English Core · Practice paper 1
subject: English Core
label: Practice paper
instr: This question paper has 18 questions. All questions are compulsory.

The paper contains three sections:
Section A: Reading Skills (22 marks), questions 1 and 2
Section B: Creative Writing Skills (18 marks), questions 3 to 6
Section C: Literature (40 marks), questions 7 to 18

The board paper has 13 questions. Here its short answer questions are given one at a time: questions 10 to 14 stand for board question 10 (Flamingo) and questions 15 and 16 for board question 11 (Vistas); questions 17 and 18 stand for board questions 12 and 13.
Attempt all questions based on the specific instructions for each part. Adhere to the prescribed word limit while answering the questions.
All the names, addresses and figures used in the questions are fictitious. Resemblance, if any, is purely coincidental.
Internal choices of the board paper are not included: each question has one version.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following passage.

1. On a summer afternoon, the air above a crowded city market can be several degrees warmer than the air above fields only a short drive away. Scientists call this difference the urban heat island effect. It is not a new discovery: it was first described in London more than two hundred years ago. Yet it has become far more serious as Indian cities have grown taller, denser and more thickly paved.

2. The main cause lies in the materials we build with. Concrete, asphalt and dark roofing sheets absorb most of the sunlight that falls on them and release the stored heat slowly through the evening and night. Trees and open soil behave differently. They cool their surroundings by giving off water vapour, a process known as evapotranspiration. When a neighbourhood replaces its trees with parking lots, it loses its natural cooler and gains, in effect, a giant storage heater.

3. Human activity adds to the burden. Vehicles, factories and the very air-conditioners that people install to escape the heat all release warm air into the streets. This sets up a cruel cycle: the hotter the city becomes, the more air-conditioners are switched on, and the more heat is pumped outside.

4. The effects are not shared equally. The heat is often fiercest in crowded settlements with tin roofs, narrow lanes and little room for greenery. Here, nights that never cool down deny the body its chance to recover from the day. Doctors point out that it is the warm night, more than the hot afternoon, that raises the risk of heatstroke, especially for elderly people, young children and those who work outdoors.

5. The remedies are surprisingly simple. A coat of white, reflective paint on a roof can make the room below noticeably cooler. Rows of shade trees along streets, protected lakes and wetlands, and paving that lets rainwater soak into the ground all help a city shed its heat. Some Indian cities have also begun to issue heat warnings in advance and to open cool shelters for people who have no fans or electricity at home.

6. Technology alone, however, will not solve the problem. Town planners argue that cooling a city calls for a change in thinking. Shade, water and green space must be seen not as luxuries but as public health infrastructure, as essential as roads and drains. A city that keeps itself cool, they say, is a city that keeps its people well.

Answer the following questions, based on the given passage.

parts.q: (i) Which detail in paragraph 1 shows that the urban heat island effect is not a recent observation?
parts.model: It was first described in London more than two hundred years ago.

points.t: Identifies that the effect was first described in London more than two hundred years ago

parts.q:
(ii) Complete the following with a suitable reason. (paragraph 2)
The writer says that a neighbourhood which replaces its trees with parking lots gains 'a giant storage heater' because ______.
parts.model: concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly through the evening and night, while the trees that cooled the area are gone.

points.t: Reason: paved surfaces absorb the sun's heat and give it out slowly through the evening and night (loss of the trees' cooling may be added)

parts.q: (iii) Why does the writer call the cycle described in paragraph 3 'cruel'?
parts.model: Because the very thing people use to escape the heat makes it worse: as the city gets hotter, more air-conditioners are switched on, and they pump even more heat into the streets.

points.t: Explains that air-conditioners used to escape the heat release more heat outside, so the problem keeps feeding itself

parts.q:
(iv) Which of the following best describes the role of evapotranspiration, as explained in paragraph 2?
A. It stores the sun's heat in the soil and releases it at night.
B. It cools the surroundings as trees and soil give off water vapour.
C. It makes concrete and asphalt reflect more sunlight.
D. It carries warm air from the city to the nearby fields.
parts.model:
B. It cools the surroundings as trees and soil give off water vapour.
[The passage says trees and open soil cool their surroundings by giving off water vapour.]

points.t: Correct option: B. It cools the surroundings as trees and soil give off water vapour.

parts.q: (v) Why are crowded settlements hit hardest by the heat? (Any one reason) (paragraph 4)
parts.model:
They have tin roofs, narrow lanes and little room for greenery, so the heat is fiercest there.
[Also accept: nights there do not cool down, so the body cannot recover; many residents have no fans or electricity (paragraph 5).]

points.t: Any one valid reason from the passage: tin roofs / narrow lanes / little greenery / nights that do not cool down

parts.q:
(vi) According to the passage, why are warm nights especially dangerous?
A. They increase the use of tin roofs in settlements.
B. They stop trees from giving off water vapour.
C. They deny the body its chance to recover from the day's heat.
D. They make it impossible to issue heat warnings in advance.
parts.model:
C. They deny the body its chance to recover from the day's heat.
[Paragraph 4: nights that never cool down deny the body its chance to recover, raising the risk of heatstroke.]

points.t: Correct option: C. They deny the body its chance to recover from the day's heat.

parts.q: (vii) How does the example of air-conditioners show that a solution for one person can worsen a problem for everyone? (Answer in about 40 words) (paragraph 3)
parts.model: An air-conditioner cools the room of the person who switches it on, but it releases warm air into the street. When thousands of people do the same, the whole city becomes hotter, which makes even more people switch on air-conditioners. Private comfort thus increases the shared problem.

points.t: Explains that an air-conditioner cools one room but pumps warm air outside
Links this to the whole city: more use makes the city hotter, which leads to still more use (shared problem worsens)

parts.q:
(viii) The writer's tone throughout the passage can best be described as ______.
A. alarmist and hopeless, suggesting nothing can be done
B. informative and solution-oriented, explaining causes and remedies
C. sarcastic and critical, mocking city planners
D. nostalgic and sentimental, longing for village life
parts.model:
B. informative and solution-oriented, explaining causes and remedies
[The passage explains causes and effects and then offers practical remedies; it is neither hopeless nor mocking.]

points.t: Correct option: B. informative and solution-oriented, explaining causes and remedies

parts.q: (ix) What do town planners mean when they say that shade, water and green space are 'public health infrastructure'? (Answer in about 40 words) (paragraph 6)
parts.model: They mean that trees, lakes and open green areas are not decoration or luxuries. Like roads and drains, they are basic services a city must provide, because they keep the city cool and so protect people from heat-related illness such as heatstroke.

points.t: States that these are essential basic services, like roads and drains, not luxuries
Explains the health link: they keep the city cool and protect people from heat-related illness

parts.q: (x) Find a word from paragraph 4 that means 'most intense'.
parts.model: fiercest

points.t: Correct word: fiercest

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following passage carefully.

1. Every few years, the transport department of Riverpur, a fast-growing city of about four million people, asks a sample of 2,000 office workers how they travel to work. The latest survey, carried out in 2025, has been compared with the one from 2019, the year before the city's first metro line opened.

2. The results, given in the table below, reveal a clear shift. In 2019, only 12 per cent of the workers used the metro; by 2025 the figure had risen to 27 per cent. Over the same period, the share of people driving cars fell from 21 to 16 per cent, and the share using two-wheelers dropped from 34 to 28 per cent. The city bus lost a little ground, while walking and cycling together stayed almost unchanged.

Mode of travel to work2019 (% of workers)2025 (% of workers)
Metro rail1227
City bus2522
Two-wheeler3428
Car2116
Walking or cycling87
Total100100

3. The survey also recorded how long people took to reach work. The average one-way journey fell from 52 minutes in 2019 to 44 minutes in 2025. Officials believe that fewer private vehicles on the main roads, along with the speed of the metro, explain much of this improvement. However, workers living far from metro stations reported little change, and many said that the 'last kilometre' between the station and their home or office was still the hardest part of the trip.

4. The survey brought out some concerns as well. Women said that well-lit stations and women-only coaches made them feel safer, but several added that the walk to the station after dark was still a worry. Older workers asked for more lifts and escalators.

5. Transport planners say the figures send a clear message. A metro line can change travel habits only when it is part of a connected network: feeder buses, safe footpaths, cycle lanes and shared autorickshaws must link homes and offices to the stations. Without them, many people will continue to depend on their own vehicles.

Answer the following questions, based on the given passage.

parts.q:
(i) What was the main purpose of comparing the surveys of 2019 and 2025? (paragraph 1)
A. To find out how the arrival of the metro has changed the way workers travel to work
B. To decide the ticket prices for the two new metro lines
C. To count the number of vehicles registered in Riverpur
D. To compare the travel habits of Riverpur with those of other cities
parts.model:
A. To find out how the arrival of the metro has changed the way workers travel to work
[2019 was the year before the first metro line opened, so the comparison shows the change since the metro arrived.]

points.t: Correct option: A. To find out how the arrival of the metro has changed the way workers travel to work

parts.q: (ii) Which mode of travel gained the most between 2019 and 2025? Support your answer with figures from the table.
parts.model: The metro gained the most: its share rose from 12 per cent in 2019 to 27 per cent in 2025, a rise of 15 percentage points. Every other mode fell or stayed almost the same.

points.t: Identification: metro rail
Justification with figures: 12% to 27% (a rise of 15 percentage points)

parts.q:
(iii) Which of the following statements is correct, according to the table?
A. Cars and two-wheelers together were used by 55 per cent of workers in 2019 and by 44 per cent in 2025.
B. The share of workers using the city bus rose between 2019 and 2025.
C. More than half the workers used the metro in 2025.
D. The share of workers walking or cycling doubled between 2019 and 2025.
parts.model:
A. Cars and two-wheelers together were used by 55 per cent of workers in 2019 and by 44 per cent in 2025.
[Cars + two-wheelers: 21 + 34 = 55 in 2019 and 16 + 28 = 44 in 2025. The bus fell (25 to 22), the metro was 27 per cent, and walking or cycling fell from 8 to 7.]

points.t: Correct option: A. Cars and two-wheelers together were used by 55 per cent of workers in 2019 and by 44 per cent in 2025.

parts.q:
(iv) In paragraph 3, the 'last kilometre' refers to ______.
A. the final stretch between the metro station and a worker's home or office
B. the last station at the end of the metro line
C. the distance a car can travel on one litre of fuel
D. the final day on which the survey was carried out
parts.model:
A. the final stretch between the metro station and a worker's home or office
[The passage describes it as the part of the trip between the station and home or office.]

points.t: Correct option: A. the final stretch between the metro station and a worker's home or office

parts.q: (v) Do you agree that the metro alone explains the fall in the average journey time? Give your view with a reason, with reference to paragraph 3. (Answer in about 40 words)
parts.model: No, the metro alone does not explain it. Officials link the improvement both to the speed of the metro and to fewer private vehicles on the main roads. Also, workers living far from stations saw little change, so the benefit depends on how close people live to a station.

points.t: Clear judgement: the metro is only part of the reason (No / not alone / partly)
Justification from paragraph 3: fewer private vehicles on main roads also helped, and/or workers far from stations saw little change

parts.q:
(vi) Which of the following is NOT discussed in the passage?
A. Safety concerns of women travelling to stations after dark
B. The need for lifts and escalators for older workers
C. The cost of metro tickets compared with the cost of fuel
D. The fall in the average time taken to reach work
parts.model:
C. The cost of metro tickets compared with the cost of fuel
[Safety, lifts and journey times are all discussed; ticket prices and fuel costs are not.]

points.t: Correct option: C. The cost of metro tickets compared with the cost of fuel

parts.q:
(vii) Fill in the blank with the correct option from those given in brackets.
According to the planners in paragraph 5, a metro line works best as part of an ______ network. (isolated / integrated / expensive)
parts.model:
integrated
[Paragraph 5: feeder buses, footpaths, cycle lanes and autorickshaws must link homes and offices to the stations.]

points.t: Correct word: integrated

parts.q: (viii) Meena lives four kilometres from the nearest metro station, and her office is next to a station. Using paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, give two reasons why she may still prefer to ride her scooter to work. (Answer in about 40 words)
parts.model: First, the 'last kilometre' (in her case four kilometres) from home to the station is the hardest part of the trip, and workers far from stations gained little. Second, without feeder buses, safe footpaths or cycle lanes linking her home to the station, people like her continue to depend on their own vehicles. (Also accept: the walk to the station after dark is a worry for women.)

points.t: Reason 1 with reference to the passage (e.g. distance from home to the station / 'last kilometre' problem)
Reason 2 with reference to the passage (e.g. no feeder bus, footpath or cycle lane link; or safety worry after dark)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: You are Aarav/Anika Sharma, Secretary of the Eco Club of Greenfield Public School, Lucknow. The club is organising an e-waste collection drive in the school. Draft a notice in about 50 words for the school notice board, informing students about the drive and inviting volunteers. Include the necessary details. Put your notice in a box.
questions.model:
[In a box]
GREENFIELD PUBLIC SCHOOL, LUCKNOW
NOTICE
15 January 2027
E-WASTE COLLECTION DRIVE
The Eco Club will hold an e-waste collection drive on Monday, 25 January 2027, from 8:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. at the main gate. Bring old phones, chargers, cables, batteries and other unused electronic items; they will go to an authorised recycler. Volunteers may give their names to the undersigned by 20 January.
Anika Sharma
Secretary, Eco Club

points.t: Format: box, name of the school, the word NOTICE, date of issue, heading, and name with designation at the end (half mark if one or two of these are missing)
Content: what (e-waste collection drive), when (date and time) and where (venue)
Content: items to be brought and what will be done with them, and how to volunteer (whom to contact, last date)
Accuracy of spelling and grammar

questions.subject: English
questions.text: You are Ritika/Rohan Iyer, Head Girl/Head Boy of Sunrise Senior Secondary School, Pune. Your school is holding its annual science exhibition on the theme 'Science for a Greener Tomorrow'. Draft a formal invitation in about 50 words to Dr Meera Kulkarni, a retired space scientist, requesting her to inaugurate the exhibition and address the students. Include the essential details.
questions.model:
Sunrise Senior Secondary School, Pune
The Principal, staff and students
request the pleasure of the company of
Dr Meera Kulkarni
as the Chief Guest at the inauguration of the
Annual Science Exhibition: 'Science for a Greener Tomorrow'
on Friday, 12 February 2027, at 10:00 a.m.
in the school auditorium.
Dr Kulkarni is also requested to address the students after the inauguration.
RSVP: Ritika Iyer, Head Girl
Phone: 98XXXXXX10

points.t: Format: formal invitation in the third person, name of the host, name of the guest, and RSVP with name and contact (half mark if one or two of these are missing)
Content: the occasion (science exhibition and its theme) and the guest's role (to inaugurate it and address the students)
Content: date, time and venue
Accuracy of spelling and grammar

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Many public libraries in your city are in poor condition and are hardly used, though they could be of great help to students and other residents. You are Kavya/Kabir Malhotra of 27, Civil Lines, Bhopal. Write a letter in 120-150 words to the Editor of a local newspaper, drawing attention to the problem and suggesting ways to revive the libraries.
You may use the following cues:
- present condition of the libraries
- who loses when libraries are neglected
- repairs, new books and digital facilities
- longer opening hours
- role of residents, schools and local businesses
questions.model:
27, Civil Lines
Bhopal
8 March 2027
The Editor
The Central Chronicle
Bhopal
Subject: Need to revive the city's public libraries
Sir/Madam
Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the sorry state of our public libraries.
Most of them have broken furniture, poor lighting and leaking roofs. Their collections have not been updated for years and there is no internet access. As a result, few people visit them, although many students cannot afford books or a quiet place to study at home.
The Municipal Corporation should repair these buildings and add new books, newspapers and computers. The libraries could stay open till late evening so that students and working people can use them. Residents, schools and local businesses could donate books and volunteer their time, and reading clubs could be started for children.
A well-kept library is a gift to the whole community. I hope the authorities will act without delay.
Yours truly
Kavya Malhotra

points.t: Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, complimentary close 'Yours truly' and name
Organisation of ideas: purpose stated in the opening, the problem and suggestions in separate paragraphs, a suitable conclusion
Content: the problem described with details (condition of the libraries and who loses because of it)
Content: at least two practical suggestions (e.g. repairs and new books or computers, longer hours, help from residents, schools and businesses)
Accuracy of spelling and grammar

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Every year many lives are lost because no one nearby knows what to do in the first few minutes after an accident or a sudden illness. You are Sana/Sahil Verma, a Class XII student of Modern Public School, Indore. Write an article in 120-150 words for your school magazine on why every student should learn basic first aid.
You may use the following cues:
- the 'golden hour' after an accident or emergency
- common situations: burns, cuts, fainting, choking
- confidence and calm in a crisis
- how schools can teach first aid
- a trained student as a helper in the community
questions.model:
FIRST AID: A SKILL EVERY STUDENT NEEDS
by Sana Verma, Class XII
An accident on the road, a classmate who faints in the assembly, a younger brother who chokes on a sweet: emergencies arrive without warning. The first few minutes, often called the golden hour, can decide whether a person survives.
Basic first aid is easy to learn. Cooling a burn under running water, pressing a clean cloth on a bleeding cut, placing a person who has fainted in a safe position, or helping someone who is choking are simple steps that can save a life before the doctor arrives.
First aid also teaches us to stay calm instead of panicking. Schools can hold short courses with doctors and the Red Cross, keep first-aid kits in every block and run regular practice drills.
A trained student becomes a helper wherever he or she goes. Learning first aid is not just a lesson; it is a responsibility.

points.t: Format: a suitable title and the writer's name (byline)
Organisation of ideas: an engaging introduction, ideas developed in paragraphs, a conclusion
Content: why first aid matters (golden hour, common emergencies with examples)
Content: benefits and suggestions (staying calm; how schools can teach it; helping the community)
Accuracy of spelling and grammar

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following extract.

Aunt Jennifer's tigers prance across a screen,
Bright topaz denizens of a world of green.
They do not fear the men beneath the tree;
They pace in sleek chivalric certainty.
(Aunt Jennifer's Tigers, Adrienne Rich)

parts.q:
(i) Complete the following by choosing the correct option from those given in brackets.
The word 'prance' suggests that the tigers move with ______. (confidence and joy / fear and caution / anger and violence)
parts.model: confidence and joy

points.t: Correct option: confidence and joy

parts.q:
(ii) Complete the following appropriately.
The tigers are called 'denizens of a world of green' because ______.
parts.model: they are shown living in the green forest (jungle), their natural home, which Aunt Jennifer has embroidered on the screen.

points.t: Explains that the tigers are inhabitants of the green forest/jungle shown on the screen

parts.q:
(iii) The 'men beneath the tree' most probably stand for ______.
A. hunters, and more widely the power of men that could threaten the tigers
B. gardeners looking after the forest
C. artists who taught Aunt Jennifer to sew
D. travellers resting in the shade
parts.model:
A. hunters, and more widely the power of men that could threaten the tigers
[The tigers' fearlessness before the men suggests freedom from male power, which Aunt Jennifer herself lacks.]

points.t: Correct option: A. hunters, and more widely the power of men that could threaten the tigers

parts.q:
(iv) The phrase 'sleek chivalric certainty' presents the tigers as ______.
A. graceful, noble and sure of themselves
B. wild, cruel and dangerous
C. tired, slow and old
D. timid, nervous and hesitant
parts.model:
A. graceful, noble and sure of themselves
['Sleek' suggests grace, 'chivalric' suggests the dignity of knights, and 'certainty' suggests confidence.]

points.t: Correct option: A. graceful, noble and sure of themselves

parts.q: (v) What does the word 'topaz' suggest about the way Aunt Jennifer has made the tigers?
parts.model: Topaz is a bright yellow gemstone, so the word suggests that she has embroidered the tigers in bright, shining yellow thread. They look vivid, precious and full of life.

points.t: Bright, gleaming yellow like a gem: the tigers are vivid and precious / full of life

parts.q: (vi) How do the tigers on the screen contrast with the woman who created them?
parts.model: The tigers are bold, free and fearless, while Aunt Jennifer is timid and weighed down by an oppressive marriage. Through them she expresses the freedom and courage she lacks in her own life.

points.t: Contrast: tigers fearless and free / Aunt Jennifer timid and oppressed (the tigers express what she lacks)

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following extract.

"You are to come to the palace," the man said. "The old General is in pain again."
"Oh," Hana breathed, "is that all?"
"All?" the messenger exclaimed. "Is it not enough?"
"Indeed it is," she replied. "I am very sorry."
When Sadao came to say goodbye, she was in the kitchen, but doing nothing. The children were asleep and she sat merely resting for a moment, more exhausted from her fright than from work.
"I thought they had come to arrest you," she said.
(The Enemy, Pearl S. Buck)

parts.q:
(i) The word 'breathed' in 'Hana breathed' suggests that she spoke ______.
A. loudly and angrily
B. softly, almost under her breath
C. mockingly, to tease the messenger
D. in a trembling scream
parts.model:
B. softly, almost under her breath
[To 'breathe' words is to say them very quietly; her soft reply also shows her sudden relief.]

points.t: Correct option: B. softly, almost under her breath

parts.q:
(ii) Complete the following appropriately.
The messenger's reply, "Is it not enough?", shows that to him the General's illness ______.
parts.model: is a matter of the greatest importance, and he is shocked that anyone could treat it lightly.

points.t: Shows the General's illness is very important to him / he is shocked by Hana's light response

parts.q: (iii) Why was Hana 'more exhausted from her fright than from work'?
parts.model: Because she and Sadao were secretly sheltering a wounded American prisoner of war in their house, she lived in constant fear of being found out. This tension drained her more than any household work.

points.t: Links her exhaustion to the fear of discovery because they were hiding the American prisoner of war

parts.q:
(iv) Complete the following by choosing the correct option from those given in brackets.
The extract shows that Hana and Sadao were living in a state of ______. (constant anxiety / calm confidence)
parts.model: constant anxiety

points.t: Correct option: constant anxiety

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following extract.

"I am thinking of this stranger here," said the young girl. "He walks and walks the whole year long, and there is probably not a single place in the whole country where he is welcome and can feel at home. Wherever he turns he is chased away. Always he is afraid of being arrested and cross-examined. I should like to have him enjoy a day of peace with us here - just one in the whole year."
The ironmaster mumbled something in his beard. He could not bring himself to oppose her.
(The Rattrap, Selma Lagerlof)

parts.q:
(i) The girl speaks these words to ______.
A. the peddler himself
B. her father, the ironmaster
C. the crofter
D. the sheriff
parts.model:
B. her father, the ironmaster
[She speaks of 'this stranger here' in the third person, and it is the ironmaster who 'could not bring himself to oppose her'.]

points.t: Correct option: B. her father, the ironmaster

parts.q:
(ii) Complete the following appropriately.
The repetition in 'He walks and walks the whole year long' suggests ______.
parts.model: the endless, tiring and aimless wandering of a man who has no home to go to.

points.t: Endless / tiring / aimless wandering of a homeless man

parts.q: (iii) What does the phrase 'just one in the whole year' add to the girl's request?
parts.model: It stresses how small her request is: she asks for only one peaceful day against a whole year of wandering and fear. This makes her plea moving and very hard for her father to refuse.

points.t: Shows how modest the request is (one day against a whole year of hardship), which makes it moving / hard to refuse

parts.q:
(iv) The girl's wish to give the stranger 'a day of peace' is linked to the time of year at which the story takes place. That time is ______.
A. Christmas
B. the girl's birthday
C. New Year's Day
D. a harvest festival
parts.model:
A. Christmas
[The peddler is brought to the manor at Christmas time; the ironmaster even speaks of letting the sheriff alone on Christmas Eve.]

points.t: Correct option: A. Christmas

parts.q:
(v) Complete the following appropriately.
The girl looks at the stranger not as a suspicious vagabond but as ______.
parts.model: a lonely, hunted fellow human being who deserves warmth and a little peace.

points.t: A lonely / hunted human being who deserves kindness (her compassion)

parts.q: (vi) How does the girl's attitude in this extract prepare the reader for the change in the peddler at the end of the story?
parts.model: She treats the peddler with trust and kindness, as a human being and not as a thief. This kindness later awakens the good in him, so that he returns the money he had stolen and signs himself Captain von Stahle.

points.t: Her kindness and trust awaken his better self, leading him to return the stolen money (and sign himself Captain von Stahle)

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Answer in 40-50 words.
In 'Lost Spring', garbage means different things to the children and to the elders of Seemapuri. Explain the difference. What does it show about their lives? (Lost Spring)
questions.model: For the elders, garbage is a means of survival: it is their daily bread and a roof over their heads, so 'garbage to them is gold'. For the children it is wrapped in wonder, as finding a silver coin gives them hope of finding more. Poverty has made rubbish the centre of their lives.

points.t: Content: for the elders garbage is a means of survival (daily bread, a roof over their heads)
Content: for the children it is wrapped in wonder (hope of finding a coin); shows how poverty shapes their lives, even childhood
Expression: a clear, relevant answer of about 40-50 words with accurate grammar and spelling

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Answer in 40-50 words.
Even after months of practice with an instructor in the pool, Douglas was 'still not satisfied'. What did he do next, and what does this reveal about the way he overcame his fear of water? (Deep Water)
questions.model: Traces of the old terror still returned, so he was not sure that all of it had left. He swam two miles across Lake Wentworth, where the terror returned only once, and at Warm Lake he swam across and back without fear. He conquered fear by testing himself again, with determination and persistence.

points.t: Content: he was not sure all the terror had left, so he tested himself alone in open water (Lake Wentworth, where it returned only once; Warm Lake)
Content: fear conquered through repeated self-testing, determination and persistence
Expression: a clear, relevant answer of about 40-50 words with accurate grammar and spelling

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Answer in 40-50 words.
Gandhi opposed the idea of taking C.F. Andrews' help in the Champaran struggle. Do you think he was right? Give reasons from the chapter. (Indigo)
questions.model: Yes. Gandhi felt that leaning on Andrews showed the weakness of their hearts and that they must rely on themselves. By refusing, he taught the people self-reliance, which was central to his idea of freedom: in everything he did, he tried to mould a new free Indian who could stand on his own feet.

points.t: Content: seeking Andrews' help showed the weakness of their hearts; they had to rely on themselves
Content: a judgement with reason: the refusal taught self-reliance, Gandhi's idea of freedom (a free Indian standing on his own feet)

'The Last Lesson' shows how people value something only when they are about to lose it. Discuss with reference to Franz, the villagers and M. Hamel.
questions.model:
In 'The Last Lesson', the order from Berlin that only German is to be taught in the schools of Alsace makes everyone value French just as they are losing it.
Franz, who had not learnt his participles and was tempted to spend the day out of doors, now feels bad about his neglect. M. Hamel does not scold him; he says that all of them have a great deal to reproach themselves with.
The village elders sit on the back benches. Their presence shows that they too have realised, too late, what they are losing.
M. Hamel, dressed in his formal clothes for the last lesson, calls French the most beautiful language in the world, the clearest and the most logical. He asks them to guard it, because for an enslaved people their language is the key to their prison.
The story teaches us to value our language before it is taken away.

points.t: Content: the order from Berlin; Franz's change - from neglecting his lesson on participles to feeling bad about it
Content: the villagers on the back benches - their late realisation of the value of French

'The Tiger King' is a satire on the arrogance of people who hold absolute power. Discuss with reference to the Maharaja's actions.
questions.model:
Kalki's 'The Tiger King' mocks the vanity of the Maharaja of Pratibandapuram, who believes his power can defeat fate.
Told that his hundredth tiger will cause his death, he bans tiger hunting by anyone except himself, threatens to confiscate the property of anyone who harms a tiger, and vows to attend to other matters only after killing a hundred tigers.
He refuses a high-ranking British officer permission to hunt and, to save his throne, sends fifty diamond rings to the officer's wife at a cost of three lakh rupees. He even marries a princess from a state with a large tiger population.
Yet fate wins. His hundredth tiger, an old animal brought by the dewan, only faints and is killed by one of the hunters. Finally, a wooden toy tiger bought for his son's birthday causes his death.
The satire shows that absolute power cannot conquer destiny.

points.t: Content: the prophecy and his arrogant response - ban on tiger hunting for all others, threat of confiscation, vow to kill a hundred tigers
Content: misuse of power and wealth - refusing the British officer, fifty diamond rings costing three lakh rupees / marriage for tigers
Content: the ironic ending - the hundredth tiger only fainted and was killed by a hunter; death caused by the wooden toy tiger; power cannot defeat fate
